chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Husayn ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'It is upon you to keep company with the person of intellect, even if you do not praise his generosity — but benefit from his intellect and guard yourself from his evil manners. And do not abandon the company of the generous person, even if you do not benefit from his intellect — but benefit from his generosity using your own intellect. And flee, with all manner of fleeing, from the lowly fool.'

key_terms.احْتَرِسْ: Guard/be cautious — to protect oneself proactively, not merely passive avoidance
key_terms.اللَّئِيمُ الْأَحْمَق: The lowly fool — combining moral baseness (la'im) with intellectual deficiency (ahmaq); the worst combination
key_terms.الْفِرَارُ: Fleeing — the emphatic construction (flee all manner of fleeing) conveys the urgency of complete avoidance
key_terms.الْكَرِيم: The generous/noble person — one characterized by magnanimity and nobility of character
key_terms.ذَا الْعَقْلِ: The person of intellect — one endowed with reason and wisdom

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali say about choosing companions based on intellect and generosity?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) transmits a teaching from Imam Ali (AS) distinguishing three types of people and prescribing different social strategies for each. The intelligent person should be kept as company for his wisdom even if he lacks generosity, the generous person for his kindness even if he lacks intellect, but the lowly fool should be avoided entirely. This hadith reflects the early Islamic emphasis on beneficial companionship as a tool for self-improvement, recognizing that virtue in a companion need not be complete — even partial virtue yields benefit.
